newsitem.title: POLAND: Czech-style growth slump unlikely in Poland - finmin.
newsitem.headline: Czech-style growth slump unlikely in Poland - finmin.

text.p: Finance Minister Marek Belka on Wednesday said Poland was unlikely to experience a slow-down in economic growth, which hit its southern neighbour, the Czech Republic.

Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said this month his country's 1997 GDP growth would be at best only half of the 5.4 percent envisaged in this year's budget, even after implementation of a recently-adopted revival package.
The slump follows several years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and a sharp rise in wages provoked a consumer boom.

Asked if this scenario could take place in Poland, where the economy has enjoyed a 5-7 percent growth in the last three years but recently exerienced a rise of credit action and consumer spending, Belka said:
"No, I do not think so... We pursue a different macroeconomic policy, but there also is another reason -- adjustments on microeconomic level to the market economy went much farther (in Poland)."

He said Poland's monetary policy had been tighter and, unlike in many other countries of the former Soviet bloc, wages in enterprises had grown much slower than labour efficiency and firms' profitability.
He also said Poland was less vulnerable than the Czech Republic to an economic slow-down because it had better regulated its capital market.

These regulations may have resulted in slower privatisation than in the Czech Republic but the quality of sell-offs was better and legal safeguards enforced better corporate governance of privatised companies, Belka said.
Analysts say that with exports growth well behind imports growth in early in the year, Poland's trade deficit is likely to widen to more than $12 billion in 1997 from $8.2 billion last year.

But Belka and many analysts earlier said high imports growth posed no threat to Poland's growth, forecast at 5.5 percent this year, because the country bought mainly investment goods and components for production rather than consumer goods.

Analysts also say Poland's current account gap, seen at 3.5 percent of the gross domestic product or $4-5 billion this year against one percent of GDP last year, is still relatively small for a developing economy.
